Self-proclaimed pastor and former cult leader Paul Mackenzie is escorted out of the Mombasa High Court in Mombasa, Kenya, 06 November 2026 [Stringer/EPA]By Al Jazeera Staff, Reuters and The Associated PressPublished On 27 Nov 202627 Nov 2026
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.

Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.
Earlier convictions
On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.
He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.
The Shakahola deaths
Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.

The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.
Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.

US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.

Street vendors wait for customers at their spice stall in the southwestern city of Taiz, Yemen [Anees Mahyoub/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 27 Nov 202627 Nov 2026
Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and takes on occasional domestic work to feed her family. Rising prices have changed how she shops. “Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera.
Food is still on the shelves. It was available in the markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment. Across Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent, or $91, more that month than in August, its highest level in a year.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemenlist 2 of 3Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen governmentlist 3 of 3The escalation in Yemen is a turning pointend of list
Families on both sides of the front lines are struggling, and prices are rising faster in the government-held south, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). What sets the Houthi-controlled north apart is how little families there can earn and how little help is left.
Most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work a month, FEWS NET reported in October. The UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025, FEWS NET said. Maria Corina Machado launching her neighbourhood assemblies initiative in Caracas on Thursday [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 27 Nov 202627 Nov 2026
Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.
The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US appeals court lets Trump end TPS deportation protections for Venezuelanslist 2 of 3Protesters clash with police over Venezuela’s poor minimum wagelist 3 of 3Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spendingend of list
“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.
The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.
An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.
Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.

OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.
The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Apple files lawsuit accusing ChatGPT maker OpenAI of stealing trade secretslist 2 of 4John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 yearslist 3 of 4Elon Musk’s X Corp and SpaceXAI drop antitrust lawsuit against Applelist 4 of 4How AI apps are offering free substitutes for Big Tech softwareend of list
OpenAI is developing artificial intelligence-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf,” the company said in its Friday court filing.
OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware products.
“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.
Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

Vladimir Putin at the flag-raising ceremony for the new Yasen-M nuclear-powered submarine on Friday (Sputnik pool foto/AFP)By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 27 Nov 202627 Nov 2026
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.
The Russians say they will add five more nuclear submarines to the country’s fleet by 2030.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Russian cargo ship leaves Finland’s territorial waters after drone attacklist 2 of 3Russia warns Ukraine of ‘dangerous trend’ after Libya and Baltic attackslist 3 of 3‘We’ll keep sinking Russian ships’: Ukraine challenges Putin’s global reachend of list
Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm at the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk on Friday, marking the submarine’s formal transfer to the navy, according to video released by the Kremlin.
“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” he said.
Nuclear-powered subs are a key part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.
Putin said the navy will receive five more submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class, the same as the Perm. They can operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.
Putin also stated that Russia intends to continue modernising its navy and expressed confidence that all plans to build a powerful naval force will be implemented in full and on time.

item.title: Is Iraq facing renewed instability?
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration 28 minutes 10 seconds play-arrow
28:10Read more
Roughly 20 percent of Iraq’s oil reserves are in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
The local government runs the oil fields and revenue helps it govern. But now that is in danger.
The federal government has announced control over refineries. Baghdad says it’s losing millions of dollars every month to crude oil smugglers.
That’s united the Kurds who are bitterly opposed to the move. Thousands have protested against what they say is a loss of autonomy.
Are their fears justified? Will the deployment of government troops on the border lead to a military confrontation?
Presenter: Rishaad Salama
Guests:
Sajad Jiyad – Political analyst and senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy
